answers.text: The brief says only 'our managed secret store' and does not name the product or the identity mechanism. The plan assumes the platform hands the pod an identity with no static credential (for example workload identity), but which product and mechanism is not known. Added to the assumptions, and step 1 now records both and step 2's probe verifies them.

Yes, always the latest version. Each write creates a new version id, so a corrected value written later is a new latest version. Running pods fetch the latest every 5 minutes and swap it in, so they adopt it within about 5 minutes with no restart. Stated in steps 4 and 14.

Yes. deploy.md says a new pod must pass its readiness probe, GET /healthz returning 200, before an old pod is stopped. The HTTP server starts only after the keys load, so before that the probe cannot connect and the pod counts as not ready, and the rollout halts. Added to step 15.

Look at the first new pod's outbound calls to the three providers in the central logs or metrics and compare its error rate with the old pods. Stop and roll back on any 401 or 403 from a provider or a clearly higher error rate. Soak length and the exact threshold are left to the team. Added to step 7.

The line is logged once per refresh cycle, for example secrets_refreshed pod=orders-api-abc12 payments_api_key=v7 email_api_key=v3 geocoding_api_key=v5. Query the central log service (30-day retention) for it and group by the pod field, then compare to the cluster pod list. The exact format can change but must carry the pod name and all three version ids. Added to steps 17 and 8.

The charge call returns the provider error to its caller and logs a warning. The given files do not show whether the order is then marked failed or who retries it; that is existing order code which this plan does not change. Added as an open question for the orders-api team.

Preferred order: approve PR, deploy the PR-branch image to staging, run drills, merge, deploy to prod. If the pipeline cannot deploy a PR-branch image, merge first (CI builds on merge to main), deploy that image to staging, and hold the prod deploy until the drills pass. Merge never happens before step 4. Clarified in step 6, and step 7 now starts after the merge.

Yes. deploy.md says CI bakes config/app.yaml exactly as in the repo into each image, and images are immutable, so the old image keeps its own copy of the YAML with the old keys. Removing the keys in the new PR does not touch images already built. This is also why step 9 blocks rollback to pre-migration images after revocation. Added to step 7.

answers.text: Rollback is a redeploy of the previous image, as deploy.md already defines; the rolling rules keep ready pods serving, and the new pods are replaced one at a time by old-image pods. The engineer running the deploy decides and tells the security on-call. Safe because old keys are not revoked yet. Added to step 7.

Not known where each provider shows last-used or how stale it is; the brief does not say. Step 1 now records both per provider, and step 8 check 3 requires the margin to exceed that recorded lag. Added as an open question for the security on-call.

Secret is a wrapper around the key string: printing it shows <redacted> and reveal() returns the real string. The secrets provider is the one process-wide object that owns the snapshot, the get(name) call and the refresher thread; the snapshot is the immutable map it currently holds. Clients hold a reference to the provider. Defined in step 15.

Each secret is handled independently. The snapshot still swaps in the new values of the ones that succeeded and keeps the previous value of the one that failed. The secrets_refreshed line shows the older version id still in use for the failed one, and a WARNING is logged. Added to step 17.

A forced re-read that finds a new version updates the shared snapshot for that secret, so all other requests use it too, not just that call. The 5-minute timer is unaffected and keeps running; the forced re-read is rate-limited to once per 30 seconds per secret. Added to step 16.

Pre-migration images are those built before the merge commit of the migration PR. Step 8 check 1 has already shown that no running pod uses one, and a rescheduled pod pulls the image named in the current deployment, which is the new one, so removing them does not affect running pods. Added to step 9.

Staging uses sandbox keys, never live ones, so no live key is needed there once migrated. Staging pods still on the old image keep using the old keys from their YAML until the staging rollout replaces them; new staging pods read staging/*. The staging identity is separate from the prod one with the same shape, read-only on staging/* only, and cannot read prod. Clarified in steps 2, 3 and 6.

answers.text: Only an old-image pod holds an old key, and step 8 check 1 (image digest) catches any such pod. A new-image pod, silent or paused, holds the new key from the store. Check 2 now says a pod whose latest secrets_refreshed line is older than one interval plus a margin fails, so a stuck or silent pod is caught even if its last line looked right. Check 3 (provider last-used) catches any caller outside the pod list, for example a script. Added a line to step 8 saying how the three checks cover each other.

Not quite straight away. First, if the snapshot already holds a different version than the request used, it retries once with the snapshot value, with no store call. If the version is the same and a re-read was done for that secret in the last 30 seconds, it skips the re-read and returns the provider error with a warning, because a fresh re-read just showed no newer version. Rewritten as numbered cases in step 16.

The pod uses the identity the platform provides (step 13). Failing to obtain that identity is treated as a failed fetch and follows the same retry path: wait 2 seconds, up to 3 retries, then exit non-zero. Added to step 14.

Yes. The old image loads only config/app.yaml (existing config_loader.py) and has no store code, so old pods never call the store. A store outage affects only new pods starting up. Added one clause to step 7.

The expected version is the latest version id in the store at the time of the check, read as metadata only. It must match the ticket's record, and step 4 already requires the ticket to be updated on a corrected write. If they differ, find out why before passing the gate. Added to step 8 check 2.

Watch two signals: the provider's record of rejected attempts on the suspended key, which names the caller, and orders-api's own provider 401 or 403 rate against normal. Any rejected attempt on the old key means a missed caller, so re-enable. A rise in orders-api 401s with no rejected attempt on the old key points at something else, such as the new key, so investigate that first. Whether each provider exposes rejected attempts is not known; step 1 now records it per provider. Added to steps 1 and 10.

teachbacks.text:
I'll follow two things: one pod's life (Part 1), then the rollout that puts it in production (Part 2).

**Part 1: one new pod, from start to a customer request**

1. The container starts. The app reads `config/app.yaml`, which now holds only non-secret settings (`base_url`, timeouts, `from_address`, port, log level). It also reads `APP_ENV`, a plain name (prod, staging or dev). If `APP_ENV` is missing, or an `api_key` is in the YAML, the process exits non-zero before it listens.

2. Initial load. The HTTP server is not up yet, so no customer request can arrive. The app calls the managed secret store as the pod's platform identity (`orders-api-prod` in prod, which can only read `orders-api/prod/*`). It fetches the latest version of `payments_api_key`, `email_api_key` and `geocoding_api_key` under `orders-api/$APP_ENV/`. Each call returns a value and a version id, and each has a timeout of about 3 seconds. If any fetch fails, including failing to get the identity, it waits 2 seconds and retries only the missing ones. That gives up to 3 retries, so at most 4 attempts. The values are held in process memory only. If it still fails, it logs the secret names and error class (never values) and exits non-zero. During a rollout the pod never becomes ready, so the rollout halts and the old pods keep serving. Outside a rollout the orchestrator restarts the container.

3. Publish the snapshot and go ready. The three keys go into the first snapshot, an immutable map `{name: (Secret, version_id)}` owned by the secrets provider. The app logs one line per secret with name and version id only. It starts the refresher thread, then starts the HTTP server. If the refresher can't start, the process exits before the server starts. `GET /healthz` returns 200 only while the snapshot holds all three keys. Before the server listens, the probe can't connect, which counts as not ready. `/healthz` does not turn unhealthy when a later refresh fails. Once the pod is ready, the rolling deploy may stop an old pod.

4. A customer request makes an outbound provider call, such as `PaymentsClient.charge`. The clients hold a reference to the secrets provider, not a key. On every call the client does `self._secrets.get('payments_api_key')`, which reads the current snapshot. It then calls `reveal()` on the `Secret` wrapper and puts the string in the `Authorization` header. A request already in flight keeps the value it read. On a 401 or 403 from the provider, the client retries at most once:
   - If the snapshot now holds a different version than the request used, it retries with the snapshot's value. No store call is made.
   - Otherwise, if no forced re-read of that secret happened in the last 30 seconds, it re-reads that one secret from the store (3 second timeout). If there is a new version, it puts it in the shared snapshot and retries once with it.
   - Otherwise it returns the provider error and logs a warning.

   If the store is unreachable during that re-read, the request returns the provider error and the cached value stays in use.

5. Refresh. Every 5 minutes the refresher thread fetches the latest version of each secret, each handled on its own. A new version id goes into a new snapshot that is swapped in atomically, and the app logs `secret_rotated name old_version new_version`. An unchanged id does nothing. A fetch error, or an empty or malformed value, keeps the previous value for that secret, while the other secrets still update. It logs a WARNING with the name, error class, version in use and time since the last good load. Readiness stays 200. After every cycle it logs a `secrets_refreshed` line with the pod name and all three version ids in use. The confirmation gate in step 12 reads that line.

6. Stop or restart. On SIGTERM, a crash or a reschedule, memory is discarded and nothing is persisted. A new process repeats steps 1 to 3.

7. Local development. `make run` sets `APP_ENV` to dev and reads `orders-api/dev/*` with the engineer's own login, which holds sandbox keys. The loader refuses `APP_ENV=prod` outside the prod identity. `make run-offline` uses a fake backend with placeholder values and local provider stubs. Tests use the same fake backend.

**Part 2: the rollout that gets there with no customer failures**

8. Inventory. The team lists every caller of the old keys: environments, CI, scripts and laptops. They use the providers' last-used data to find callers nobody listed. They confirm each provider allows two valid keys at once and offers sandbox keys. They record the store product, the identity mechanism, and how the providers show last-used time, lag and rejected attempts. If a provider allows only one active key, they stop and escalate. An unknown caller joins the scope and blocks the gate.

9. Create the store layout. There is one KMS key per environment. The paths `orders-api/prod/*`, `orders-api/staging/*` and `orders-api/dev/*` are reserved. Access is set so that `orders-api-prod` can read prod only, only the security on-call can write prod, staging has its own read-only identity, and engineers get read-only on dev. A probe secret at `orders-api/prod/_probe` verifies these permissions and the identity mechanism.

10. Issue and store new keys. The security on-call creates new keys at each provider while the old ones stay active. The values go from the provider console straight into the store. Each new key is tested with a harmless read-only call, and sandbox keys are also created. The on-call writes the prod secrets interactively, so no value appears on a command line. Each write returns a version id, and those ids are recorded in the ticket as the expected versions.

11. Build and review the PR. It contains the runtime changes from Part 1 and these rollout pieces:
    - The `api_key` lines are removed from the YAML.
    - The loader fails if `api_key` appears in the YAML.
    - A CI check blocks `api_key` and the `pk_live_`, `ml_live_` and `geo_live_` patterns in `config/app.yaml`.
    - `Secret` redaction.
    - Tests, including one asserting a sentinel key never appears in logs or `os.environ`.

    It must not merge before step 10.

12. Staging, then prod.
    - Staging: deploy to staging and run the failure drills (store down at startup, a new version adopted within 5 minutes, a blocked refresh, a revoked sandbox key, and a check of logs and `os.environ`). Then merge and do the prod rolling deploy.
    - Prod: the deploy runs one pod at a time with `maxUnavailable: 0`. Each new pod loads the keys as `orders-api-prod` and reports ready, and only then is an old pod stopped. New pods use the new keys. Old pods use the old keys baked into their image. Both keys are valid, so no request fails. After the first new pod, the team pauses and compares its provider error rate with the old pods. They roll back on any 401 or 403 or a clearly higher error rate. The engineer running the deploy decides to roll back and tells the security on-call.

13. Confirmation gate before revocation. Three checks are recorded in the ticket:
    1. Every pod, job and script runs the new image digest.
    2. For every live pod, the latest `secrets_refreshed` line shows the expected store versions. A silent or stale pod fails.
    3. Each provider shows the old key's last-used time older than one refresh interval plus a margin that exceeds the provider's lag, with no unknown callers.

    If any check fails, nothing is revoked until the stragglers are fixed and the gate is repeated.

14. Block old images. Pre-migration images are marked non-deployable and removed from the registry, because after revocation they would fail every provider call. If this can't be done, nothing is revoked.

15. Revoke the old keys, one provider at a time, in the order geocoding, email, payments. If the provider supports suspension, suspend first and watch for one refresh interval, then delete. The signals watched are the provider's rejected-attempt record on the old key and orders-api's own 401 and 403 rate. A rejected attempt means a missed caller. If one appears, the team re-enables the suspended key if the provider allows, finds the caller and repeats the gate for it. Deletion is irreversible, so it happens only after a clean suspension. Sign-off from the security on-call and one engineer is required.

16. Afterwards, the team opens a throwaway PR to prove the CI guard blocks an `api_key` line. They search 30 days of central logs for the live-key patterns, rotating and purging any key found. They write a runbook and hand the rotation-cadence question to security. Later rotations repeat steps 10, 13 and 15. They issue and store the new key, wait up to 5 minutes, run the gate, then revoke.
gaps: What the order code does after a provider call finally fails (marks the order failed, who retries it). The document says this is unspecified existing behavior.
What the 'harmless read-only call' used to test each new key is for each provider.
The refresh failure alert threshold ('several cycles') is left to on-call.
The soak length and error-rate threshold for the first-new-pod pause are left to the team.
The secret store product and the identity mechanism are unnamed, so I can't explain how a pod authenticates concretely.
Where each provider shows last-used time and rejected attempts, and how stale that data is, is unknown until rollout step 1 records it.
The document does not say how a new key's rollout step 10 (suspend or delete) is handled for a provider with no suspend option beyond 'delete only after a clean suspension'.
It is not stated how pod names are obtained for the `secrets_refreshed` line, nor which log system is 'central logs'.
